And further, a third merit is that he is saved from a strange death, as they said in the Zohar (Parashat Miketz, page 201b) concerning a certain man who had this merit and was saved from a strange death - these are its words: Rabbi Abba was sitting at the gate of Lod, and he saw a certain man coming to sit in a hollow hanging from the ground - he was weary from the road and sat and slept there. Meanwhile he saw a serpent coming toward him; a weasel came out and killed the serpent. When that man awoke, he saw that serpent before him, dead, and that man stood up, and that hollow fell into the depth beneath him, and he was saved. Rabbi Abba came to him and said, tell me what your deeds are, for the Holy One, blessed be He, performed for you these two miracles - they are not for nothing. That man said to him, all my days no wicked person has ever completed his day against me without my having made peace with him and forgiven him - and moreover, if I was unable to make peace with him, I would not go up to my bed until I had forgiven him and all who troubled me, and I would not worry, all day, about the evil that had happened to me; and it was not enough for me, but from that day onward I would strive to do good to them. Rabbi Abba wept and said, this man's deeds are greater than Joseph's - Joseph's were certainly his brothers, and it was fitting for him to have mercy on them, but what this one does is greater than Joseph, and it is fitting that the Holy One, blessed be He, perform for him miracle upon miracle - to this point.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:18-2: And further, among the category of the merit of humility is what is said in Kiddushin (71a), that the [Explicit] Name is transmitted only to whoever is in the middle of his years and is not angry. And I heard a story from the pious Rabbi Yaakov Ashkenazi, of blessed memory, that he was a wondrous sage in wisdom, and wished to teach his wisdom to Rabbi Yehoshua the Pious, but first tested him regarding anger - for it was a tradition in their hands not to transmit the wisdom except to one who, when tested with anger, would not become angry - and he tested him six times, and he endured, but on the seventh he did not stand firm, and so on.

The tenth merit, which is the cause of all the merits mentioned, is that the Shechinah rests with the humble and the lowly, as explained in Sotah (5a), which we copied above (chapter 1), and the Shechinah flees from the proud and the angry, as explained above (chapter 2).

And so it is further explained in the Mechilta (Parashat Yitro) - these are its words: "and Moses drew near to the thick darkness" (Exodus 20:18) - what caused him this? His humility, as it is said (Numbers 12:3), "and the man Moses was very humble" - its ultimate purpose is to cause the Shechinah to rest with man on earth, as it is said (Isaiah 57:15), "thus says the High and Exalted One who inhabits eternity, and holy is His Name; high and holy I dwell, and with the contrite and humble of spirit," and it says (ibid. 61:1), "the spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me to bring good tidings to the humble; He has sent me to bind up the brokenhearted," and it says (ibid. 66:2), "for all these My hand has made... and to this one I look, to the poor and contrite of spirit" - "the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit" (Psalms 51:19).

And whoever is proud of heart causes the land to be defiled and the Shechinah to depart, as it is said (Psalms 101:5), "haughty of eyes and proud of heart, him I cannot [endure]" - and every proud heart is called an abomination, as it is said (Proverbs 16:5), "every proud heart is an abomination to the LORD" - and idolatry is called an abomination, as it is said (Deuteronomy 7:26), "and you shall not bring an abomination into your house" - just as idolatry defiles the land and causes the Shechinah to depart, so whoever is proud of heart defiles the land and causes the Shechinah to depart - to this point. And I heard, in the name of the Midrash, a proof that the proud are hated before Him, blessed be He, in that He commanded (Leviticus 2:11), "for no leaven and no honey shall you burn as an offering" - and the reason is that honey boils in fire and produces foam, and likewise leaven boils and rises, and this is an allusion to the proud - therefore no fire-offering to the LORD shall be made from it.

It follows that pride and anger resemble each other in this punishment - for just as the angry person defiles himself, being like idolatry, as explained, so he too causes the Shechinah to depart, like the angry person.

And after a person contemplates all the merits belonging to one who is humble, lowly, and does not insist on his own rights, as we have explained, he shall see with his intellect's eye that it is far more fitting for him to bear a small suffering for a great reward, than to lose all the merits mentioned in a single moment, and come to cause great loss - that his soul and the Shechinah depart from him - and until he returns, how much toil is needed until the spirit of impurity departs from within him, as explained in the Zohar, which said, "would that he be sanctified," and said, "and once it has fled from him once, how much must a person do until it returns to its place" - and thus a sinner shall lose great goodness.

And this is a parable of a person who has in his hand a pitcher of water and a skin of balsam oil, and some trouble befalls him, and he must necessarily release from his hand one of them, which shall be lost - is it not certainly the way of reason that he sacrifice the small loss, which is the pitcher of water, in order to gain the great profit, which is the balsam in his hand? And if he does the opposite, he is certainly a fool. In exactly this manner is the matter of anger: for if a person endures not responding to his own disgrace, and forgoes the honor of his body, which is a small loss - not a loss at all, from the eye of reason - he shall gain a great profit for the level of his soul, that his transgressions shall be forgiven him, as we have elaborated in the other merits mentioned.

Further, another way so that he not come to anger is that he think that the sufferings through which sins are atoned are two different aspects: either accepting suffering upon himself through fasts, sackcloth, and ashes, as King David, peace be upon him, did, or through the death of children, which is an atoning altar, as is known - and likewise death itself atones for everything, even the profanation of the Name, when repentance preceded it, as explained in the divisions of atonement that Rabbi Yishmael used to expound (Yoma 86a). Now, all these are difficult for a person to bear, and are very bitter, especially the death of children or one's own death - and behold, a person mortifies himself with mortifications for the atonement of his sins, and sometimes these involve neglect of Torah and neglect of prayer - how pleasant it would be for him to accept light sufferings that involve no neglect of Torah and prayer, and to accept them with love for the atonement of his sins, and to rejoice when they disgrace and shame him, knowing that the Holy One, blessed be He, loves him in sending him such light sufferings in order to purify his sins. And that one who disgraces him shall bear his own iniquity, for he is an evil strap used to strike this one, as it is said (Isaiah 10:5), "woe, Assyria, rod of My anger," and so on.

And it is fitting that he pray to the Holy One, blessed be He, in all his prayers - morning, afternoon, evening - that the Holy One, blessed be He, grant him the merit of the attribute of humility and submission, and that he be joyful in these sufferings if he is shamed and provoked, and in all the other attributes of humility written in this Gate, and pray for all of them - and through this he shall be reconciled to the Holy One, blessed be He, and atonement shall be granted him for what he has sinned until now in anger and pride. And since this is his request, he shall not become angry and shall not respond to whoever disgraces him. These two ways to acquiring humility I heard from the mouth of my teacher, peace be upon him.

And I further heard that it is impossible for a person to attain the merit of holiness and repentance until he acquires in his heart the attribute of humility properly and the attribute of anger departs from him entirely - for one of the twenty-four things that delay repentance is being a wrathful person. And further, that he shall toil greatly to attain the acquisition of holiness, and when he becomes angry for a single moment everything departs, and it is found that all his toil was for naught and all his days were spent in vanity - and when he returns in repentance he shall toil greatly until he is sanctified, and would that he be sanctified - and if he becomes angry again, he has lost all he did and toiled in vain, as explained, and there is no end to the matter, that he acquire holiness through it, until he acquires through it the attribute of humility in its completeness, with the conditions to be explained in it.

And Rabbeinu Tam wrote in Sefer HaYashar (Gate 6) that the wise, when they enter repentance, should swear a severe oath not to become angry, and he elaborated on this. And I say that the oath should be only not to become angry except over a matter that the Torah permitted to be angered by, such as against the wicked, as King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 139:21), "do I not hate those who hate You, LORD, and loathe those who rise against You" - and likewise to be angry with a student, as it is said (Ketubot 103b), "cast bile among the students" - and if he becomes angry over other matters, he shall fine himself with a known penalty that shall cause him distress, and not release himself from his oath, to fulfill what is said (Psalms 15:4), "he swears to his own harm and does not retract." And he should conduct himself this way for a year or two, until he acquires through it the attribute of humility.

And I further say that it is good for a person to make a short reminder of the punishments of anger and pride, and the merits of humility, to read them every day - this device is also a fine one, for who is the fool who would wish to sustain great loss for a small gain? Rather, at the time of anger he forgets all the punishments and all the merits he shall lose - and when he persists in reading, the learning shall bring him to action, and he shall be diligent and careful.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:30-4: And I say further, that this second aspect can be confirmed from the teaching of our Rabbis, of blessed memory, in the Midrash (Shemot Rabbah, Parashat 34), on the verse (Exodus 25:10), "and they shall make an ark of acacia wood" - these are their words: Elihu came and said (Job 37:23), "Shaddai, we cannot find Him, exalted in power" - whoever hears this verse says, perhaps this is a blasphemy, God forbid - rather, Elihu meant this: we did not find the power of the Holy One, blessed be He's might, exercised with His creatures, for the Holy One, blessed be He, does not come with burdens against His creatures; He does not come upon a person except according to his own strength. You find that when the Holy One, blessed be He, gave the Torah to Israel, had He come upon them with the full force of His power, they would not have been able to withstand it, as it is said (Deuteronomy 5:22), "if we hear again," and so on - rather, He came upon them only according to their own strength, as it is said (Psalms 29:4), "the voice of the LORD is with power [bakoach]" - it does not say "with His power" [bekocho] but "with power" [bakoach] - the power of each and every one - to this point.

And from this teaching is understood the rebuke I wrote in the name of my teacher, peace be upon him: for if they say to a person, why did you not perform mortifications and fastings, he may say that he did not have the strength for them, and the Holy One, blessed be He, does not come with burdens against His creatures - but if they say to him, why did you become angry and cast off from yourself the fear of Heaven, what shall he answer his Creator? Is his evil inclination not something that must be overcome, and is it not within a person's own power over it, without any mortification at all, but merely that he take it to heart and accept upon himself that he not be exacting and not insist on his own rights? For (Psalms 10:12/Deuteronomy 10:12), "what does the LORD your God ask of you" - for fear is with you, so much so that you need not seek after it through a loss of money and the like, matters that are external to you.

And there is further confirmation for my teacher's rebukes in the verses of the Prophets and the Writings - the first, what the prophet wrote (Zephaniah 2:3), "seek righteousness, seek humility." And further what is said (Lamentations 3:30), "let him give his cheek to the one who strikes him; let him be filled with disgrace; let him put his mouth in the dust."

And further he should think of what King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 15:4), "despised in his own eyes and rejected [nim'as]" - for it is known that if he is despised in his own eyes and thinks himself rejected, he shall not respond to his own disgrace. And "rejected" is that he think of the inferiority and lowliness of his own soul, that he is rejected in the eyes of the Creator because of his evil deeds; and further, that he think of his own repulsiveness in his life and in his death - whether, in life, from the worms and lice on his head, as they, of blessed memory, explained (see Kohelet Rabbah 5:12), "how much more so man, who is a worm" (Job 25:6) - these are the lice on the head; and in his death, "the son of man, a worm" (ibid.) - being repugnant from the aspect of decay and the foul odor within his own bowels, as they, of blessed memory, explained, that at the time a person enters the privy, they say to him, see your own end - and when he thinks of this, certainly he shall not respond to his own disgrace.

And with this intent the Tanna said (Avot, chapter 4, mishnah 4): Rabbi Levitas, a man of Yavneh, says, be exceedingly, exceedingly lowly of spirit, for the hope of man is the worm. And many explanations have been said of this mishnah, and it appears to me that in saying "for the hope of man is the worm," since we hold that anything destined to be done is considered as already done - if so, since the hope of man is to become entirely worm, he should think that already, while still alive, he is partly worm - and the proof is the lice on the head, as they, of blessed memory, explained in the Midrash, "how much more so man, who is a worm" - these are the lice on the head. And once he thinks of this, he shall be lowly in his own soul's eyes, for if he considers himself, when insulted, as already dead and full of worms, he shall not pay attention to what is said, for he shall think in his heart and say, would a dead man, full of worms, respond to his own disgrace? Certainly he would not respond, for that would be outside of reason.

Further, my teacher wrote a way to acquire humility, which is that he should always strive to flee from honor, and choose the lowliest of places, and likewise strive to honor all creatures, poor and rich alike, treating them as equal - for there is no difference between the rich and the poor except in money, but both were created in image and likeness - and whoever honors creatures honors the supernal Craftsman who made them in His likeness, and if, God forbid, he disgraces them, it is as though he disgraces the Craftsman who made them - along the lines of what they said in Tractate Ta'anit (20b) concerning Rabbi Elazar, who encountered a very ugly man, and so on, and said to him, go to the craftsman who made me and tell him, how ugly is this vessel You have made - until he had to ask his forgiveness, and he said to him, I forgive you, forgive me. Further, that he always think of his own disgrace, his lack of understanding, his repugnant decay, and that he is worm and maggot.

Further, I heard from his mouth that when they disgrace and shame him, he should think that Samael stands accusing him above, and that this is a strap drawn from him - for it is written (Proverbs 16:7), "when the LORD is pleased with a man's ways, He makes even his enemies be at peace with him" - and therefore King David, peace be upon him, for the atonement of his sin, was silent when Shimi ben Gera disgraced him, calling him a man of blood (II Samuel 16:7), an adulterer, a bastard, wicked, an oppressor, an abomination - as Rashi, of blessed memory, explained on (I Kings 2:8), "and he cursed me with a severe [nimretzet] curse" - an acrostic, as explained [see above 17:42] - for he knew that Shimi was an agent from above to strike him with his tongue, and in his deeds, that he threw dust, and so on (II Samuel 16:13), and he said, for the LORD told him to curse David - and who shall say, why have you done so? - therefore he should worry about his own sins and not respond to his own disgrace.

And along these lines the pious author wrote in Chovot HaLevavot, Gate 5 (Gate of Unity of Deed, chapter 5), that this is the matter of (Avot, chapter 3, mishnah 10), "whoever is pleasing to people is pleasing to the Omnipresent" - for whoever is good in His eyes, blessed be He, the Holy One, blessed be He, plants His love in the eyes of creatures, that they love him. It follows that if they disgrace him, it is fitting for him to be silent, for certainly the spirit of the Omnipresent is not pleased with him, and he should worry about his own sins.

Further, he should think that everything his disgracer says of him is true, that he has not said even one part in a thousand of his sins - as the liturgical poet said, "if my neighbors reproved me for my sins, they would flee and distance themselves far from my borders" - and although they harm him, their harm does not reach what he himself has blemished above, for he has not taken as severely as he himself has done, being a slanderer separating an intimate friend [see Proverbs 16:28] - and how can he ignore the great war that Samael wages against him over his sins, and be preoccupied with the small war? This is what I have heard.

And I say a great rebuke for acquiring humility, and for not responding to his own disgrace, and not becoming angry - it is a parable of a certain man who went to the king and entreated him, prostrating himself before him, that he come to dwell with him - and the king, out of his great humility, agreed to dwell with him in his house. As time passed, this man performed disgraceful acts before the king, until the king fled from him. Would it not certainly be a disgrace to such a man, and should we not say of him that he is far from the discipline of decent people? For by doing those things before the king, he is found to have driven the king from his house by force - for the king cannot bear that a chamber pot of filth be brought before him until he flees, or that they crown a servant in his place and expel the king - and it was he himself who had entreated the king to come dwell with him.

And the parable's meaning is understood: for we, the people of Israel - all our prayers, our mitzvot, and our Torah are to draw the Shechinah to dwell with us, as it is said (Exodus 25:8), "and let them make Me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them" - among them literally, within their own hearts. And this premise is explained in the Zohar, the Tikkunim, and in several places, that Israel "form the image" [tzarin tzurah] - and so in the Zohar (Parashat Terumah, page 133a), that whoever prepares a bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp for the Holy One, blessed be He, the Holy One, blessed be He, shall be his guest every day, and it explains there the matter in the secret of prayer; see there. And it is known that the King's dwelling is a broken and crushed heart, as we have explained, and its opposite is anger and pride.

It follows that the angry person crowns the servant who denies the foundational principle, and expels the Shechinah that had dwelt in the soul within his heart - and therefore the soul departs, and likewise the Shechinah, as explained - and therefore the Shechinah, without doubt, shall not dwell with a person who casts her from her place and expels her whenever he wishes, but rather, once the Shechinah knows with certainty that he has already accepted upon himself not to become angry again, then she shall return to dwell with him - and this is what Rashbi, peace be upon him, said in the teaching from Parashat Tetzaveh (page 182a) that we copied above, "only if the person comes and uproots it entirely and forever, and afterward strives to sanctify himself and draw holiness upon himself" - meaning, drawing the holiness of his soul that departed from him, and likewise drawing the Shechinah, for the dwelling of the Shechinah is in the soul.

And for the reason of this parable, together with Rashbi's teaching, peace be upon him (Zohar, Parashat Beshalach, page 55b), which we copied in the Gate of Love, chapter 6, concerning "your friend and your father's friend" - see there. And this parable is also a moral lesson for all the sins by which a person sins against the Shechinah, for certainly he thereby expels her from himself, since all transgressions are the stench of the husk, and a king cannot bear anything but a good scent from Torah and mitzvot. And this is what it said there, on the verse (Proverbs 25:17), "let your foot be rare in your neighbor's house" - "let your inclination be rare," so that it not boil against you and not rule over you, and so on, as explained there, that through every deed of the evil inclination, which he gives it dominion over him, he drives away the holy soul and the Shechinah from him - and this is not fitting, since He is "your friend and your father's friend," as explained there, that He wishes to dwell with you - that you should perform deeds that would drive Him from your house.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:6-17: And I found written that this attribute, which was in this pious man, was also in [a certain] Rav, and it is counted among ten attributes he had, one of them being that whoever provoked him, he would go and appease him.

And so Rabbeinu Yonah, peace be upon him, wrote in Sefer HaYirah - and these are its words: be conciliatory to your brother and your fellow, and do not go to sleep at night with a quarrel between you and another person; rather, go and appease him until he is reconciled - and even if he sinned against you, seek reconciliation from him, and do not say, he sinned against me, so it is he who should appease me - subdue your inclination and go to him, so that your heart not become proud and you become an abomination before the Creator, as it is said (Proverbs 16:5), "every proud heart is an abomination to the LORD."

Further, a fourth merit: that his decree is torn up and life is added to him - that if he became ill and was near death, and they examined his deeds and found this merit for him, he is saved from death to life - and so they said in Tractate Rosh Hashanah (17a) - these are their own words: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, became ill. Rav Pappa went to inquire about him and saw that his condition was hopeless. He said to them, prepare his provisions [for burial]. In the end he recovered. Rav Pappa was ashamed to see him. He [Rav Huna] said to him, what did you see? He said to him, so it was [I thought]. He said to them, the Holy One, blessed be He, said, since he does not insist on his own rights, do not insist strictly on My part against him, as it is said (Micah 7:18), "who bears iniquity and passes over transgression" - for whom does He bear iniquity? For whoever passes over transgression - "for the remnant of His heritage." Rabbi Acha bar Chanina said, [there is] honey, but also a thorn in it - "for the remnant of His heritage," and not for all His heritage - only for one who makes himself like the remnant [i.e., humble] - to this point. And Rashi, of blessed memory, explained: "prepare his provisions" - prepare for him provisions for the road, meaning, the provision of the dead is shrouds. "Recovered" - was healed. "So it was" - death had been decreed upon me. "Does not insist on his own rights" - does not stand firm on his own claims. "Do not insist strictly against him" - do not scrutinize him. "Honey, but a thorn in it" - meaning, there is a matter of comfort here, but there is a hard thing within it that does not apply equally to all - to this point. And in the Midrash Ruth (Zohar Chadash) they brought a similar story about Rabbi Karuspedai, who became ill and was near death, and departed to that world, and was, and so on.

And in Chuppat Eliyahu they brought a story close in language, of the same matter, concerning the teaching we copied at the beginning of the chapter - three the Holy One, blessed be He, loves, and so on - these are its words: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, became ill, and lingered in that world for several nights and several days; when he returned, they said to him, Rabbi, through what were you released? He said to them, my children, happy is he who does not insist on his own rights - by the [divine] service, companies of ministering angels came and taught merit on my behalf, and it was not accepted from them, until an angel came and said, on behalf of whom are you teaching merit? Is it not on behalf of this one who never insisted on his own rights? Immediately they released me from death to life.

Further, there, close to this, they brought a wondrous story about one who does not insist on his own rights - these are its words: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak had a mound of earth within his vineyard, and he brought workers there to dig the mound - they dug it that whole day. On the second day, as they were digging, a certain man leaped from within his house and sat upon the mound and began to sway and cry out - and what was he crying out? Perhaps the resurrection of the dead has arrived, perhaps the resurrection of the dead has arrived! The workers ran and informed Rav Nachman. He came and found him. He said to him, who are you? He said to him, I am dead - perhaps the time of the resurrection of the dead has arrived. He said to him, what is your business at this mound? He said to him, did I not tell you, I am dead? He said to him, but a dead man does not decay? He said to him, did they not bring you into the house of study and read to you the Book of Proverbs, and did not Solomon say (Proverbs 14:30), "and envy rots the bones"? In my days I never insisted on my own rights, and I never harbored envy of my fellow in my heart, and I never gossiped, neither in the study hall nor in the synagogue, and I gave my heart and my eyes only to words of Torah, to fulfill what is said (ibid. 1:33), "but whoever listens to me shall dwell securely." Rav Nachman said to him, I shall build you a domed structure. He said to him, do not do anything for me, and do not remove me from this place, for I was buried with permission - rather, return the dust that was removed from over me to its place. And Rav Nachman was frightened and grieved the entire day, saying, woe to me, perhaps I have offended that dead man. Immediately he saw in a dream that he was sitting in a sukkah of myrtle branches. He immediately gave praise and thanks before the Holy One, blessed be He, and read this verse (ibid. 8:34), "happy is the man who listens to me, watching daily at my doors" - praised be the name of the King of kings of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, who withholds the reward of no creature - and if this one, who had in his hand only the reward of silence alone, and did not insist on his own rights, was repaid thus by the Holy One, blessed be He, how much more so shall the Holy One, blessed be He, repay double and doubled the reward of one who accustoms himself to the study of Torah, raises his children to the study of Torah, and walks in [divine] service and lowliness of spirit - to this point.

Further, a sixth merit: that the prayer of one who does not insist on his own rights is heard, as is proven in Ta'anit (25b) - it says there, a story of Rabbi Eliezer, who went down before the ark and said twenty-four blessings [of supplication] and was not answered; Rabbi Akiva went down and said "Avinu Malkeinu" and was answered. A heavenly voice went out and said, it is not that this one is greater than that one, but that this one does not insist on his own rights, and that one does not [i.e., does] insist on his own rights - to this point.

And further, a seventh merit: that the world endures through it, as explained in Tractate Chullin, end of chapter 6 (89a): Rabbi Ilai said, the world endures only through him who restrains his mouth at a time of quarrel, as it is said (Job 26:7), "He hangs the earth upon nothing [belimah]" [a play on "restraint," bal + peh]. Rabbi Abahu said, through him who makes himself as though he were nothing, as it is said (Deuteronomy 33:27), "and underneath are the everlasting arms" - to this point. And Rashi, of blessed memory, explained: "restrains" - stops up his mouth. "And underneath" - whoever is trodden underneath everyone else, he is the "arms of the world."

Further, the eighth and ninth merits: that he shall merit Torah, and that Elijah shall be revealed to him - for Torah is explained only to whoever is not exacting, and Elijah is revealed only to whoever is not exacting, as explained in Tractate Kallah Rabbati, Chapter "Judge Your Own Words Favorably" (chapter 5) - these are its words: Abba Eliyahu, of blessed memory, said, Torah is explained only to whoever is not exacting; I too am revealed only to whoever is not exacting - happy is whoever encounters him, and whoever sits with him, for he is assured of a portion in the World to Come - to this point.

And so, in the chapter "The Acquisition of Torah" (Avot, chapter 6), in the mishnah of Rabbi Meir, "whoever occupies himself with Torah for its own sake merits many things," and so on, it says at the end of its words, "and be modest, and slow to anger, and forgiving of his own insult" - for these things are a preparation for the acquisition of wisdom. "Modest," as it is written (Proverbs 11:2), "and with the modest is wisdom." "Slow to anger and forgiving of his own insult," for if he becomes angry his Torah is forgotten, as explained - we say in Tractate Sotah (21b): Rabbi Yochanan said, words of Torah endure only in one who makes himself as though he were nothing, as it is said (Job 28:12), "and wisdom, from where shall it be found?" - to this point his words. And one of the things through which Torah is acquired is being slow to anger with a good heart, and it appears to me that King Solomon, peace be upon him, said of this (Proverbs 14:29), "he who is slow to anger has great understanding, but he who is quick-tempered exalts folly."

And Rabbi Yitzchak of Acre, peace be upon him, wrote that he heard from the mouth of Rabbi Meir, the student of Rabbi Yosef Gikatilla, peace be upon him, that his teacher, Rabbi Yosef Gikatilla, peace be upon him, said to him, that the man whose heart moves him to repair his attributes and straighten his ways and his deeds, and to pursue humility to the utmost degree of perfection, to be insulted and not insult, to hear his own disgrace and not respond - immediately the Shechinah shall rest upon him, and he shall not need to learn from flesh and blood, for the spirit of God shall teach him - to this point, relevant here.

Further, the same author wrote elsewhere - these are its words: we found it written in the books of the Kabbalists who merited the true path, that one of the great repairs among the repairs for one who seeks knowledge of the LORD is that he be among the insulted, even by his own wife and household, whom he should not fear or be ashamed of, while he himself shall not be an insulter - all the more so with people who are not of his household, that he be insulted and not insult. And if he must reprimand [lit. insult] his household to turn them from the path of death, in which they transgress the will of the Omnipresent, and to straighten and guide them in the path of life, which is the path in which they do the will of the Omnipresent, let him reprimand in a manner that he not become angry in his heart, but let his heart always be joyful, cleaving to everything - to this point.

And so it is written in Tanna DeVei Eliyahu (Zuta, chapter 4), copied in the Yalkut, Parashat Ki Tisa (remez 391) - these are its words: the Sages taught, be humble toward every person, and toward the people of your household more than toward every person. Further, in Tanna DeVei Eliyahu, Parashat Atem Nitzavim, on the verse "it is not too wondrous for you" (Deuteronomy 30:11) - these are its words: a person should always be humble in Torah and in fear of Heaven with his father, his mother, his wife, his children, the people of his household, his neighbors, his relatives, and those distant from him, and even with a Gentile in the marketplace - so that he be beloved above and cherished below, and accepted by creatures, and fill his days and years with a good name; and through this his wife and household shall fear him, as it is said (Deuteronomy 28:10), "and all the peoples of the earth shall see that the Name of the LORD is called upon you, and they shall fear you" - to this point, relevant here. And without doubt, whoever trains himself to be insulted by the people of his household and not to insult shall be humble toward all and acquire in his heart the attribute of humility - for if in his own house, where they are subjugated under his hand, he is insulted and does not insult, all the more so with others.
